extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for newsroom practice focused on sourcing, verification, attribution, and organizational practices that produce ‘facts’ and maintain credibility under deadline pressure. Covers inter-bureau exchanges, libel avoidance, source legitimacy, and strategies for handling nonverifiable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional autonomy and territorial protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureau chiefs protect their territory and sources as private property (e.g., objecting when another bureau calls 'their' source), handling conflicts via professional courtesy rather than hierarchical appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve inter-bureau conflicts by direct, courteous contact (telephone the other bureau’s source or editor), offer reciprocal future coverage rather than escalating to superiors; this both protects sources and reduces poaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-bureau 'contracts' and reciprocal exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit and informal exchanges ('contracts') between bureaus: request that another bureau obtain information now with an understood, unstated future return favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When needed information lies in another bureau’s preserve, phone and request assistance (e.g., City Hall bureau gathers Dept. of Consumer Affairs list for Queens edition) and rely on quick transmission methods (telex); these exchanges increase speed and organizational efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in beats and resourcefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and bureaus must be flexible: 'The news net must be flexible ... Reporters must be capable of covering everything and anything while meeting deadlines. They must know where to get information as expediently as possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train reporters to handle varied occurrences, know multiple source avenues, and adapt quickly to locate facts under deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for centralized, legitimated sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters seek centralized sources, politicians, and bureaucrats rather than grass-roots or dissident leaders; they contact the powerful — those with resources to accomplish ambitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sources holding centralized information (officials, agency spokespeople) because their statements are seen as more authoritative and provide access to corroborating facts; be aware this shapes what becomes news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing determines what to ask and whom to ask
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowing what to ask influences whom one asks: The choice of sources and the search for 'facts' mutually determine each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a preliminary sense of 'the story' to guide targeted questions; framing precedes and structures fact-gathering and source selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts as professionally validated methods (credibility imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are 'pertinent information gathered by professionally validated methods specifying the relationship between what is known and how it is known' — credibility in the audience's mind is 'the sine qua non of news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newsroom-accepted verification practices (checking records, multiple sources, institutional corroboration) to maintain audience credibility and avoid professional/organizational sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel avoidance and handling legally vulnerable copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel is a major concern: vulnerable copy (e.g., on reputed crime figures) is shown to lawyers; organizations save copy in case of suits; many suits are settled to protect credibility and finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story could be libelous (accusation of crime or reputational harm), consult legal counsel, retain drafts/recordings, verify allegations carefully, and consider settlement risks; avoid unsubstantiated labels and use careful attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational verification standard (when to verify)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Identifying the appropriate source of information and deciding whether verification is necessary are situationally determined.' Accusations of crime or potentially libelous claims demand substantiation; routine claims may not require exhaustive checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the severity and news consequence (e.g., allegation of crime vs. social event) to determine verification level; use public records (marriage register, official files) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme verification for powerful/extraordinary claims (two-source rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For exceptional investigative reporting on powerful actors (Bernstein & Woodward), editorial rulings required that 'each alleged fact had to be verified by two independent sources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt higher corroboration thresholds for claims that contradict prevailing perceptions or threaten powerful individuals/institutions; institutional organizational needs may mandate this to protect outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web of facticity / mutual validation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Factuality for extraordinary claims is established by 'amassing mutually self-validating facts' — a web where 'A fact justifies the whole... and the whole validates this fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build clusters of corroborating particulars that reference one another (documents, multiple eyewitnesses, records) so that individual claims are supported within a coherent factual frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling nonverifiable facts by attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims cannot be verified in time, reporters 'record that the senator stated “A.”' Reporting that someone said something becomes the factual unit when verification is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute unverifiable truth-claims clearly (e.g., 'Senator X said...') rather than asserting them as reporter-verified facts; use quotation/attribution to signal unverifiability to readers/listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting opposing claims to maintain fairness and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid accusations of bias when a claim cannot be independently verified, present counterstatements (e.g., 'Senator said A' and 'Secretary said B') so the reporter can claim fairness and let consumers decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit and publish authoritative rebuttals or alternative assessments when reporting nonverifiable claims; this procedural balance is used as a professional shield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradations of legitimacy: legitimate, quasi-legitimate, public
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish among 'legitimate newsmakers, quasi-legitimate newsmakers, and the amorphous public'; holders of legitimated status are assumed to speak for institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sources with institutional legitimation (elected/appointed officials, agency heads); treat quasi-legitimate spokespeople with more caution and seek ways to show their representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical accretion as a legitimacy heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors used numerical accretion ('How many people does that guy represent?') to assess whether covering a group would confer quasi-legitimation; more members = more legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organizational size, membership, or demonstrable constituency as one criterion for deciding coverage intensity and attribution of representative status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three working generalizations about sources (prove reliability; privileged positions; institutional procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers generalize: (1) Most individuals have an axe to grind — to be believed they must prove reliability; (2) Some (committee heads) know more because they have more facts; (3) Institutions have procedures designed to protect themselves and contacts — interpret 'no comment' accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require demonstrated source reliability (ongoing contact/beats), favor sources with institutional access for complex information, and interpret institutional behavior in light of known procedures (e.g., 'clammed up' may imply impending action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be judicious with labels and supply supplementary facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors demanded supplementary facts to justify labels (e.g., calling someone a 'master musician' validated by playing with Sousa; 'communist propaganda' should be supported by titles of works seen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naked evaluative labels; provide supporting particulars (names, titles, documented activities) that enable readers to assess the accuracy of descriptive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotation and multiple named sources to distance reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding more quotations and names becomes a technical device to distance the reporter from assertions and create mutually validating facts; more named sources reduce libel risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple, named voices and direct quotations to corroborate claims and demonstrate objectivity/distance; use this practice to reduce legal exposure and editorial vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional memory and beat relationships to establish source reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proven reliability of sources 'necessarily favors sources met through institutionalized beats' because ongoing contact demonstrates trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate beats and continuous relationships with institutional sources to accumulate trust and rapid access to facts; lack of such history undermines reliance on ad hoc informants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational practices for legal risk management (saving copy; editorial vetting)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations 'routinely save copy' and show risky stories to lawyers; libel suits disrupt routines and cost money so prepublication vetting is standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement record-keeping, legal review for sensitive material, and editorial procedures (vetting, fact-checking) as part of routine risk management for potentially libelous stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting institutional behavior as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors infer meaning from institutional actions (e.g., police 'clammed up' leading editors to assume impending arrest) and use that institutional knowledge in news judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage knowledge of institutional procedures to interpret gaps, refusals, or official behavior as news-significant signals, while seeking corroboration where possible.
